title: The first jolt
hookLine: Seneca: a jolt of shock isn't anger yet, agreeing with it is (On Anger 2.3)
last: PATHOS — WHAT AM I TELLING MYSELF?

cards: A ship in a storm, somewhere between Greece and Italy. The Roman writer Aulus Gellius is on board, and so is a well-known Stoic philosopher. The waves get huge, and the philosopher goes white as a sheet.
When the storm passes, a rich passenger mocks him: some Stoic, you were as scared as the rest of us. The philosopher brushes him off with a sharp reply.
But when Gellius asks him, in earnest, why he went pale, he reaches into his bag, takes out a book of Epictetus, and shows him a passage. It's about primus motus.

teach.b: Here's what the passage said, as Gellius retells it. When something frightening appears, even the mind of a wise person is shaken for a moment. It flinches, goes pale, jumps.
That's not a failure; it's how a body works. What the wise person doesn't do is agree with it, go on to think: yes, this is truly terrible. The fool agrees, and adds more.

Seneca laid out the same idea in his essay On Anger. He lists things nobody chooses: a shiver when cold water splashes you, dizziness at the edge of a cliff, a blush, the hair standing up on your arms at bad news.
He calls these first movements. They happen to us. They are not yet anger, or fear.

Anger, Seneca says, comes in a second step, when the mind signs off on the jolt: I've been wronged, and they should pay. A third step follows, when it's out of control and no longer cares whether it's right.

teach.h: THE JOLT, THE YES, THE RUNAWAY.
teach.b: Three moments: the jolt, the yes, the runaway. The jolt isn't yours to stop. The yes is.
That's a relief. A flash of anger in traffic, a stab of jealousy at a friend's good news, a lurch of panic at an email, isn't proof you're a bad person or a failed Stoic.
It's weather passing through a body, and you're the one who decides whether to agree with it.
As yesterday taught, agreeing is where the story starts. Gellius says he found the answer satisfying. The philosopher had been pale.

how: Stoic practitioners treat a sudden flash of fear or anger as an involuntary first movement and pause before deciding whether to agree with it.

o: the moment anger finally boils over into rage
the first prayer a Stoic said each morning
the first flinch, before anger or fear begins

p: saw the Stoic go pale at sea

s: even the wise are shaken for a moment; they just don't agree with it.
for Seneca, anger begins when the mind agrees with the jolt
the first movement isn't anger yet; the yes is.
Seneca's examples include a shiver from cold water
also a blush, dizziness at a height, hair standing up.

games.q: you're the pale Stoic after the storm. a fellow traveler asks you, honestly, why you were afraid. what do you do?
o: show him a passage from Epictetus.
games.why: in Gellius's story he brushes off the mocker, but answers the honest question with Epictetus: even the wise flinch; they refuse to agree with the fear.

practice: Remember one jolt from the past day or two, a sharp noise, a rude message, a near miss, and feel where it landed: the chest, the stomach, the jaw. Then notice the small space right after it, before the story.
Breathe into that space; it's where the choice is.

wordCard.voice: Primus motus. Seneca's first movement: the involuntary flinch that comes before anger or fear, and isn't yet either one. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: first movement, the involuntary jolt Seneca describes in On Anger.

carryVoice: Your line: the jolt isn't me. The jolt happens to me; the yes is mine to give. Until tomorrow.
